paragraphs.text: Mitchell-Riley syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder. Its main features are neonatal diabetes, a hypoplastic or annular pancreas, duodenal and/or jejunal atresia with or without intestinal malrotation, and aplasia or hypoplasia of the gallbladder (Mitchell et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2010). Affected infants have low birth weight and may have intrahepatic cholestasis and intractable diarrhea that does not respond to pancreatic enzyme replacement. Many die in the first year of life (Smith et al., 2010; Sansbury et al., 2015). In some patients with biallelic RFX6 mutations, diabetes did not appear until childhood (Sansbury et al., 2015).

(2008) proposed that cases with neonatal diabetes, intestinal atresias, and gallbladder agenesis, and cases with overlapping patterns such as those described by Martínez-Frías et al. Both had a multiple congenital anomaly pattern of low birth weight, tracheoesophageal fistula, duodenal atresia, extrahepatic biliary atresia, hypoplastic pancreas, and hypospadias, which the authors regarded as a previously unreported autosomal recessive syndrome. The authors suggested these infants might have a milder form of the same syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Mitchell et al. (2004) described 5 infants: 2 sib pairs from 2 families and 1 isolated case. All presented with neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, jejunal atresia, duodenal atresia, and aplasia or hypoplasia of the gallbladder. One sib pair was born to consanguineous parents. One patient with a milder form survived free of insulin. The other 4 children died in the first year of life despite aggressive medical management. Pancreatic immunohistochemistry in 3 infants showed a few scattered chromogranin A-positive cell clusters but no insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin. Exocrine histology varied. The authors concluded that this combination of anomalies probably represented a new autosomal recessive syndrome caused by a genetic abnormality that interferes with normal islet development.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) reported 2 Turkish double first cousins. There was no stated parental consanguinity, but the mothers were sisters and the fathers were brothers. The first patient, a girl born at 32 weeks' gestation weighing 1.65 kg, had duodenal atresia, a jejunal web, and a Meckel diverticulum. Hyperglycemia (10.6 mmol/l) was noted at 2 years of age, and at 3 years she presented with diabetic ketoacidosis. At that time insulin was less than 2 microIU/ml, C-peptide was 0.023 ng/ml, and anti-GAD, IAA, and ICA antibodies were negative. She was admitted many times for gastrointestinal bleeding. A small intestinal resection at age 5 years showed patches of gastric heterotopia in the small bowel, after which the bleeding resolved. Her gallbladder was absent, but the rest of the biliary tract and her liver function tests were normal. Her identical twin had duodenal atresia and died at 1 month of age from complications of prematurity and surgery. The second patient, a boy born at 34 weeks' gestation weighing 1.70 kg, had duodenal atresia and midgut malrotation. He had asymptomatic fasting hyperglycemia (7.2 mmol/l) and was diagnosed with diabetes at age 6 years after presenting with hyperglycemia (16.0 mmol/l). He also had chronic iron deficiency anemia of unknown cause. No structural hepatobiliary abnormality was found. Both cousins were alive at 9 years of age. Sansbury et al. (2015) also reviewed the 8 previously reported cases with molecular confirmation. Duodenal atresia was present in all of them, with or without jejunal atresia or midgut malrotation. Gallbladder agenesis was present in 7 of 8, intrahepatic cholestasis in 7 of 8, and ascites in 1 further case. Five of the 8 children had died, all within the first year of life. In all of these earlier cases, diabetes had been diagnosed within the first 2 weeks of life.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) used homozygosity mapping followed by deep sequencing of all exons in the shared homozygous regions. The only nonsynonymous variant found in proband 2 was a homozygous ser217-to-pro (S217P) substitution in the RFX6 gene. Direct sequencing of RFX6 found mutations in 5 of 6 available probands, all inherited from carrier parents. Three were homozygous, respectively, for a splice donor site mutation in intron 2 (IVS2+2T-C), an out-of-frame deletion in exon 7, and an arg181-to-gln (R181Q) missense mutation. Proband 3 was compound heterozygous for splice site mutations in intron 6 (IVS6+2T-G) and intron 1 (IVS1-12A-G), and proband 2 was homozygous for S217P. In pancreas from proband 1 obtained at autopsy, the properly spliced RFX6 transcript was not detected. In DNA-binding assays, R181Q completely abolished DNA binding, whereas S217P only modestly reduced it. No RFX6 mutation was found in proband 6, whose DNA was unavailable; the authors considered this case most likely a phenocopy. They also found no RFX6 mutations in a case of Martinez-Frias syndrome.

paragraphs.text: In proband 2 with Mitchell-Riley syndrome, a child of second-cousin parents, Smith et al. (2010) found a homozygous ser217-to-pro (S217P) mutation in the RFX6 gene. It was identified by unbiased deep sequencing of exons in shared homozygous regions and confirmed by direct sequencing. The mutation was inherited from carrier parents. It lies between the DNA-binding and dimerization domains; it only modestly reduced DNA binding and did not affect dimer formation. The patient was alive at age 4.5 years. Sansbury et al. (2015) designated the mutation c.649T-C and identified the patient as the case reported by Chappell et al. (2008).

paragraphs.text: In 2 Turkish double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome and childhood-onset diabetes, Sansbury et al. (2015) found compound heterozygosity for 2 nonsense mutations in the RFX6 gene. One was a c.2176C-T transition in exon 17, resulting in an arg726-to-ter (R726X) substitution; the other was a c.2596C-T transition in exon 18, resulting in an arg866-to-ter (R866X) substitution. The mutations were found by targeted next-generation sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The fathers were heterozygous for R726X and the mothers for R866X, and both mutations had been inherited from the grandmothers. R726X was predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated decay. R866X, which lies within 50 nucleotides of the last exon-exon boundary, was predicted to escape it.
